'''Jürgen Arthur Knoblich''' (born 1963 in [[Memmingen]], Germany)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imba.oeaw.ac.at/fileadmin/user_upload/scientific/research/Knoblich/19-07_CV_Knoblich.pdf|title=CV Knoblich|last=Jürgen|first=Knoblich|date=|website=IMBA|access-date=}}</ref> is a German molecular biologist known mainly as a pioneer in developing [[cerebral organoid]]s. Since 2005, he is a Senior Group Leader at the [[Institute of Molecular Biotechnology]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.imba.oeaw.ac.at/research/juergen-knoblich/|title=Jürgen Knoblich - Team|last=|first=|date=|website=IMBA - Institute of Molecular Biotechnology|access-date=}}</ref> (IMBA) of the [[Austrian Academy of Sciences]] at the [[Vienna Biocenter]], where he acted as interim scientific director from 2018 to 2024.   

== Education and career ==
Knoblich<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Juergen_Knoblich|title=Juergen A Knoblich {{!}} PhD {{!}} IMBA Institute Of Molecular Biotechnology, Vienna {{!}} .|website=ResearchGate|access-date=16 July 2019}}</ref> studied biochemistry at the [[University of Tübingen]] and molecular biology at [[University College London]]. In 1989 he transferred to the [[Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology]] in Tübingen, where he completed his doctoral thesis in 1994 on the role of Cyclin proteins in controlling cell cycle progression during development. In 1994 he became a postdoctoral researcher at the [[University of California, San Francisco]], where he worked with Yuh Nung Jan until 1997. Upon his return to Europe he joined the [[Research Institute of Molecular Pathology|Research Institute of Molecular Pathology (IMP)]] in [[Vienna]], [[Austria]] as a group leader. In 2004, he moved to the newly founded [[Institute of Molecular Biotechnology]] (IMBA) in Vienna, where he was appointed deputy director in 2005 and acted as interim scientific director from 2018 to 2024.<ref>{{Cite web|title=IMBA|url=https://www.ccc.ac.at/ueber-das-ccc/kliniken-und-partner/kooperierende-benachbarte-wissenschaftliche-institutionen/imba/|website=www.ccc.ac.at|access-date=4 May 2020}}</ref> Both the [[Research Institute of Molecular Pathology|IMP]] and [[Institute of Molecular Biotechnology|IMBA]] are part of the [[Vienna Biocenter]]. Since 2021 he is chair in [[synthetic biology]] at the [[Medical University of Vienna]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Vienna|first=Medical University of|title=Jürgen Knoblich appointed Chair in Synthetic Biology at MedUni Vienna {{!}} MedUni Vienna|url=https://www.meduniwien.ac.at/web/en/ueber-uns/news/news-im-april-2021/juergen-knoblich-uebernimmt-professur-fuer-synthetische-biologie-an-der-meduni-wien/|access-date=2 July 2021|website=Medical University of Vienna|language=en}}</ref>

== Research focus ==
[[File:Querschnitt Gehirnmodell small.jpg|thumb|Cross section of a complete cerebral organoid with different brain regions. Cells are shown in blue, neural stem cells in red and neurons in green.]]
Knoblich’s research<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=knoblich j - PubMed - NCBI|url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=knoblich+j|last=pubmeddev|website=www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov|access-date=16 July 2019}}</ref> is known for the development <ref>{{Cite web|title=Eppendorf {{!}} Nature|url=https://www.nature.com/nature/awards/eppendorf|website=www.nature.com|language=en|access-date=4 May 2020}}</ref> of an [[organoid]] model of early [[Human brain development timeline|human brain development]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Dr. Jürgen Knoblich Talks Organoids|url=https://www.stemcell.com/jurgen-knoblich-talks-organoids.html|website=www.stemcell.com|access-date=19 November 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lancaster|first1=Madeline A.|last2=Knoblich|first2=Juergen A.|date=October 2014|title=Generation of cerebral organoids from human pluripotent stem cells|journal=Nature Protocols|volume=9|issue=10|pages=2329–2340|doi=10.1038/nprot.2014.158|issn=1750-2799|pmc=4160653|pmid=25188634}}</ref> together with his postdoctoral fellow [[Madeline Lancaster|Madeline A. Lancaster]]. His team was the first to demonstrate that organoids derived from human [[Cell potency|pluripotent stem cells]] (iPS cells) can be used to model human disease, a breakthrough that was ranked within the top 10 scientific discoveries in 2013 by [[Science (journal)|''Science'']] magazine.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Science's Top 10 Breakthroughs of 2013|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/sciences-top-10-breakthroughs-2013|date=19 December 2013|website=Science {{!}} AAAS|access-date=19 November 2019}}</ref>

This model is now commonly referred to as “[[cerebral organoid]]s”. It recapitulates early steps of human brain development during the first trimester and has been used by many other research groups.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jg|first1=Camp|last2=F|first2=Badsha|last3=M|first3=Florio|last4=S|first4=Kanton|last5=T|first5=Gerber|last6=M|first6=Wilsch-Bräuninger|last7=E|first7=Lewitus|last8=A|first8=Sykes|last9=W|first9=Hevers|date=22 December 2015|title=Human Cerebral Organoids Recapitulate Gene Expression Programs of Fetal Neocortex Development|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|language=en|volume=112|issue=51|pages=15672–7|bibcode=2015PNAS..11215672G|doi=10.1073/pnas.1520760112|pmc=4697386|pmid=26644564|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ma|first1=Lancaster|last2=M|first2=Renner|last3=Ca|first3=Martin|last4=D|first4=Wenzel|last5=Ls|first5=Bicknell|last6=Me|first6=Hurles|last7=T|first7=Homfray|last8=Jm|first8=Penninger|last9=Ap|first9=Jackson|date=19 September 2013|title=Cerebral Organoids Model Human Brain Development and Microcephaly|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=501|issue=7467|pages=373–9|bibcode=2013Natur.501..373L|doi=10.1038/nature12517|pmc=3817409|pmid=23995685}}</ref> Organoid models enable researches to perform studies directly on human tissues that can be grown from any human individual.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hynds|first1=Robert E.|last2=Giangreco|first2=Adam|date=March 2013|title=The relevance of human stem cell-derived organoid models for epithelial translational medicine|journal=Stem Cells|volume=31|issue=3|pages=417–422|doi=10.1002/stem.1290|issn=1066-5099|pmc=4171682|pmid=23203919}}</ref> They allow scientists to efficiently transfer research findings from fruit flies and animal models to human tissues and thus to investigate heritable genetic brain diseases on human tissue.

Since 2013 his team have developed cerebral organoids. In 2017, they showed that by fusing two separately patterned organoids it is possible to study interactions between distinct brain areas.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bagley|first1=Joshua A.|last2=Reumann|first2=Daniel|last3=Bian|first3=Shan|last4=Lévi-Strauss|first4=Julie|last5=Knoblich|first5=Juergen A.|date=July 2017|title=Fused cerebral organoids model interactions between brain regions|journal=Nature Methods|volume=14|issue=7|pages=743–751|doi=10.1038/nmeth.4304|issn=1548-7105|pmc=5540177|pmid=28504681}}</ref>

Previously, his research had also centered around the mechanisms of [[brain development]]. His were neuronal [[stem cell]]s, their asymmetrical cell division and processes of growth control. Building on his post-doctoral work, Knoblich and his colleagues characterized a complete mechanism for asymmetrical stem cell division in neural stem cells of the fruitfly [[Drosophila melanogaster|Drosophila]]. Their results were published in a series of seminal papers, including a report in [[Cell Journal|Cell]] in 2008.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Linking Cell Cycle to Asymmetric Division: Aurora-A Phosphorylates the Par Complex to Regulate Numb Localization|last1=F|first1=Wirtz-Peitz|last2=T|first2=Nishimura|date=3 October 2008|journal=Cell|language=en|pmid=18854163|last3=Ja|first3=Knoblich|volume = 135|issue = 1|pages = 161–73|doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2008.07.049|pmc = 2989779}}</ref> Until then, it was unknown how stem cells can separate into a self-renewing daughter cell and a specialized differentiating cell at the same time. [[Asymmetric cell division]] is based on a reaction cascade in which a cascade of molecular switches are activated or inactivated. [[Protein]]s in this cascade are either turned “on” or “off” depending on their [[phosphorylation]] state, starting with a [[kinase]] that transfers the first phosphate residue, named [[Aurora A kinase|aurora kinase A]]. Aurora kinase A is often over-expressed in [[tumor cells]], alongside other molecules that also play a role in the process of asymmetric cell division. Since stem cell mitosis is a highly conserved process, results found in fruit flies can be transferred to humans and thereby help to gain insights into general tumor neogenesis<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Linking Cell Cycle to Asymmetric Division: Aurora-A Phosphorylates the Par Complex to Regulate Numb Localization|last1=F|first1=Wirtz-Peitz|last2=T|first2=Nishimura|date=3 October 2008|journal=Cell|language=en|pmid=18854163|last3=Ja|first3=Knoblich|volume = 135|issue = 1|pages = 161–73|doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2008.07.049|pmc = 2989779}}</ref>

Additionally, Knoblich and his group were the first to carry out a genome-wide in vivo [[RNA interference|RNAi screen]] to demonstrate for the first time, that it is possible to simultaneously analyze gene functions across the whole genome of an organism in a tissue specific manner.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Genome-wide Analysis of Notch Signalling in Drosophila by Transgenic RNAi|last1=Jl|first1=Mummery-Widmer|last2=M|first2=Yamazaki|date=23 April 2009|language=en|pmid=19363474|last3=T|first3=Stoeger|last4=M|first4=Novatchkova|last5=S|first5=Bhalerao|last6=D|first6=Chen|last7=G|first7=Dietzl|last8=Bj|first8=Dickson|last9=Ja|first9=Knoblich|journal=Nature|volume=458|issue=7241|pages=987–92|doi=10.1038/nature07936|pmc=2988197|bibcode=2009Natur.458..987M}}</ref> This was achieved using a [[Drosophila melanogaster|fruit fly]] [[gene bank]] generated at [[Institute of Molecular Biotechnology|IMBA]] by [[Barry Dickson]], in which every single one of the approximately 13,000 fruit fly genes can be inactivated in any cell independently.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mummery-Widmer|first1=Jennifer L.|last2=Yamazaki|first2=Masakazu|last3=Stoeger|first3=Thomas|last4=Novatchkova|first4=Maria|last5=Bhalerao|first5=Sheetal|last6=Chen|first6=Doris|last7=Dietzl|first7=Georg|last8=Dickson|first8=Barry J.|last9=Knoblich|first9=Juergen A.|date=23 April 2009|title=Genome-wide analysis of Notch signalling in Drosophila by transgenic RNAi|journal=Nature|volume=458|issue=7241|pages=987–992|doi=10.1038/nature07936|issn=1476-4687|pmc=2988197|pmid=19363474|bibcode=2009Natur.458..987M}}</ref> With this method, Knoblich could further investigate brain tumor development in fruit flies. Recent findings suggest that tumors can be based on stem cells, that keep their unique stem cell characteristics and thus uncontrollably divide, without ever differentiating into specific somatic cell types. This lack of differentiation is caused by [https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/Q8MQJ9 Brat], a [[gene]] that has been identified by Knoblich and his team.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The Tumor Suppressor Brat Controls Neuronal Stem Cell Lineages by Inhibiting Deadpan and Zelda|last1=I|first1=Reichardt|last2=F|first2=Bonnay|date=January 2018 |language=en|pmid=29191977|last3=V|first3=Steinmann|last4=I|first4=Loedige|last5=Tr|first5=Burkard|last6=G|first6=Meister|last7=Ja|first7=Knoblich|journal=EMBO Reports|volume=19|issue=1|pages=102–117|doi=10.15252/embr.201744188|pmc=5757284}}</ref>
